analysis.one_liner: Requires the Pentagon to clean up "forever chemical" contamination to the strictest applicable water standard.
analysis.headline: The bill to force stricter Pentagon cleanup of PFOS and PFOA in drinking water died in committee without a single vote, cosponsor, or hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Department of Defense to clean up PFOS and PFOA—two "forever chemicals" linked to health harm—left in drinking water and groundwater by military and National Guard activities. Cleanup would have to reach the strictest standard that applies: a federal rule, a federal health advisory, or a state standard, whichever is toughest. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents living near military bases and National Guard facilities whose drinking water or groundwater is contaminated with PFOS or PFOA. The bill would require the Pentagon to clean that water to the most stringent standard in effect—federal or state—rather than the minimum, which matters because some states have set limits far tighter than federal health advisories. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near military bases with contaminated water

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Defense to clean PFOS and PFOA contamination from drinking water and other groundwater to the most stringent applicable standard—whichever is toughest among enforceable state standards, enforceable federal standards, and federal health advisories—rather than a weaker minimum.
Covers contamination from both Department of Defense and National Guard activities, including groundwater that is not currently used for drinking water, so future water sources would also be cleaned.
Includes a savings clause that leaves all other Superfund (CERCLA) rules and liabilities untouched, so the bill only raises the cleanup level and does not weaken existing law.

analysis.who_pays: The Department of Defense, and ultimately federal taxpayers, would bear the cost of cleaning military sites to the strictest applicable standard. States with tough limits and communities near bases would see faster, deeper remediation; the bill contains no separate funding, so the cost competes with other defense spending priorities. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill sets no deadlines and provides no dedicated funding, so the Pentagon could meet the stricter standard slowly or by shifting money from other defense needs.

It is narrow: it covers only PFOS and PFOA—two of thousands of PFAS chemicals—and only contamination from Department of Defense or National Guard activities, leaving industrial and other sources of the same chemicals untouched.

Requiring cleanup to the strictest standard in any relevant jurisdiction could raise remediation costs substantially at military installations nationwide, a cost an honest supporter would have to justify against competing uses of the defense budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in scope: cleaner drinking water for the specific communities around military and National Guard sites with PFOS or PFOA contamination, aimed at chemicals linked to serious health concerns. The cost—deeper remediation paid from the defense budget—is a legitimate public expenditure rather than a transfer to any private interest, and the bill carefully leaves existing Superfund liability law alone. Its main weakness is design, not direction: no deadlines, no funding mechanism, and only two chemicals covered mean the help could have been slow even if it had passed.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in September 2020 with no cosponsors, it was sent to three House committees and then a subcommittee, and nothing further ever happened before Congress adjourned in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Elissa Slotkin introduced the bill on September 11, 2020—less than two months before the end of the session—with no cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to three committees at once: Armed Services, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure.

Three days later it was referred to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, and no committee action, vote, or floor consideration ever followed before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Pentagon is better off, since it never faced a binding requirement to clean contaminated sites to the strictest state or federal standard. Communities near military installations with PFOS and PFOA in their water gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Pentagon and its cleanup budget

for.name: Rep. Elissa Slotkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring stricter Pentagon cleanup of PFOS and PFOA contamination; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Chairmen of the Armed Services, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have made the Pentagon pay for deeper remediation of PFOS and PFOA contamination at its own and National Guard sites, holding it to the toughest state or federal standard rather than the minimum. As the polluter and the payer, its institutional interest was in avoiding that mandate.

industries.industry: Public water systems and private well owners near military bases
industries.note: Water suppliers and households drawing from groundwater near installations would have received cleanup to the strictest applicable standard, lowering treatment burdens and exposure risk. Their interest ran directly with the bill's purpose.
